extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (PR managers/planners)
extracted.subtask_description: Translating broad organizational or PR goals into concrete, measurable public relations objectives (communication effects) using management-by-objectives and selecting appropriate PR models and evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations contributes to organizational effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations helps other subsystems communicate among themselves and with external publics and thus contributes to organizational effectiveness by helping the organization control and adapt to its environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness can be conceived in two ways: (1) attaining organizational goals and (2) surviving/adapting and acquiring resources from the environment. PR contributions should be justified in terms of how they help attain goals or enable survival/adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define organizational effectiveness in context (goals vs. natural-systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational effectiveness is variously defined as goal attainment or as successful survival/adaptation within the environment; no single universal goal applies to all organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize many possible organizational goals (productivity, efficiency, profit, quality, adaptation, growth, job satisfaction, information management, etc.). Because goals vary, PR cannot be judged by a single universal standard—objectives must be linked to the organization's current goals and environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate PR goals into concrete objectives using Management by Objectives (MBO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use MBO to reformulate organizational goals into unit and individual goals and as measurable standards against which actual performance will be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top PR managers should work with middle managers to define program goals (press relations, employee relations, government relations, community relations); middle managers should work with subordinates to develop individual objectives. Objectives should be stated as expected results (communication effects) so performance can be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make objectives measurable and focused on communication effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all public relations programs are communication programs; therefore the effects to be measured should be communication effects (knowledge, attitudes, behavior, relationships, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ill-defined, unreasonable, and unmeasurable communication objectives commonly stated by practitioners. Ground objectives in communication theory and research so they are specific and measurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on the Domino Theory (message → knowledge → attitude → behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume a simple, inevitable sequence in which message exposure produces knowledge, which produces attitude change, which then produces behavior change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research shows the dominos rarely topple in a predictable sequence. Do not design objectives or evaluate PR as though cognitive effects will automatically cascade into affective and conative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Hierarchy of Effects concept cautiously (cognitive / affective / conative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication effects can be categorized as cognitive (awareness/knowledge), affective (attitudes/evaluation), and conative (behavior/action), but the assumed stairstep order is often too simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting objectives, specify which type(s) of effect are targeted but do not assume they will occur in a fixed order; empirical evidence and theory indicate the sequence is not guaranteed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize multiple kinds of media/communication effects (content/time × effect type × level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media effects are multidimensional: effects may arise from content or from time spent with media, can be cognitive/affective/conative, and can operate at individual, interpersonal, or societal levels (Chaffee's 18 kinds; McLeod & Reeves' matrices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select which specific effect(s) your objective targets (e.g., content-driven cognitive effect on individuals vs. diffuse time-driven macro effect). Don't treat 'attitude change' as a single monolithic target—be precise about content/time, effect type, and system level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for selective exposure and relevance in audience targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Receivers seek messages relevant to them and selectively expose themselves to consonant information; dissonance theory and later refinements show people don't passively receive messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design objectives and strategies that consider how and why target publics seek information (relevance) and the likelihood they will expose themselves to your messages; targeting and timing are critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be realistic about the persuasive power of mass media
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners often overestimate media power; communication scholars emphasize limited effects and reinforcement of existing beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting objectives, avoid promising profound attitude or behavior change solely from media exposure. Use research-based expectations about what media can accomplish (e.g., agenda-setting, awareness, reinforcement) and combine with interpersonal/other channels as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose PR model aligned with organizational environment and objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Select among press agentry/publicity, public information, two-way asymmetric, and two-way symmetric models according to the organization's environment and goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly competitive environments tend to produce press agentry/publicity or two-way asymmetric uses of PR (environmental control). Less competitive environments tend toward public information and two-way symmetric models (adaptation). Use the contingency model to choose the appropriate model for stated objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide between environmental control (persuasion) and adaptation (understanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication can be used to attempt to control other groups (persuasion) or to adapt to them (understanding); PR goals should reflect which is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptive goals (social responsibility, public understanding, two-way communication) align with the two-way symmetric model and are chosen when key publics or PR professionals are in the dominant coalition. Control goals align with press agentry or two-way asymmetric approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure PR goals become organizational goals via dominant coalition inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: PR goals are more likely to become organizational goals when the PR department or key external publics are part of the organization's dominant coalition (those with central and indispensable power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If PR or relevant publics are excluded from the dominant coalition, it will be difficult to justify PR's value to top management regardless of achievement of communication objectives. Strategies for greater inclusion and demonstrating indispensability can help elevate PR goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use coorientation measures as symmetric communication objectives (congruence, accuracy, understanding, agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coorientation assesses the joint orientation of organization and public via: congruence (perceived similarity), accuracy (how well perceptions match reality), understanding (extent ideas are the same), and agreement (extent evaluations align).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-way symmetric objectives should emphasize increasing accuracy and understanding (and where possible agreement). Empirical research shows communication most frequently increases accuracy, less often understanding, and least often agreement. Use activities (e.g., community meetings) that foster mutual exchange to raise these measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish objectives that affect publics from objectives that change organization–public relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: PR can target effects on a single person or group (micro) or target the relationship between the organization and publics (interpersonal or systemic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, articulate whether the objective is to change a public's cognition/attitude/behavior or to improve the relationship (coorientation measures). Relationship-level objectives often require two-way symmetric communication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: When excluded from the dominant coalition, justify PR via environmental control objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: If PR executives and key publics are not part of the dominant coalition, PR may need to justify its function through environmental control (persuasion) objectives rather than adaptive goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of influence in such circumstances; frame short-term persuasive objectives to demonstrate value and build credibility for later inclusion and more adaptive goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground objectives in communication theory and research rather than practitioner myth
rubrics_metrics.description: Many practitioners hold extreme views of communication power; communication science offers nuanced, research-based models (Hovland, dissonance, Chaffee, McLeod & Reeves) to inform objective-setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult relevant theories and empirical findings when drafting objectives (e.g., selective exposure, multiple media effects, coorientation). This reduces unrealistic promises and produces measurable, defensible objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify the system level and measurement indicators for each objective (individual, interpersonal, macro)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects operate at micro (individual), interpersonal (relations), and macro (community/society) levels; measurement and objectives must match the chosen level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate indicators and methods depending on level (surveys for individual knowledge/attitudes, network analysis or coorientation surveys for relationships, media or social indicators for societal effects). Be explicit about level in objectives to ensure measurable evaluation.
